LECTURE 00

How to Use This Note
এই নোটের উদ্দেশ্য: পরীক্ষায় দ্রুত recall + technically correct answer + sketch-driven presentation

     Exam Strategy প্রতি Section-এ ৪ সেট থেকে ৩ সেট উত্তর করতে হবে। তাই Section A-তে “সবকিছু অল্প” না পড়ে
     ৩টি শক্ত set + ১টি backup set প্রস্তুত করো। এই নোটে Very High / High priority প্রশ্নগুলো সেই উদ্দেশ্যে সাজানো
     হয়েছে।

Answer-writing pattern (10-20 marks)
1.    Definition / core concept - 2 to 3 lines.
2.    Key factors / mechanism - bullets or a compact table.
3.    Necessary sketch - labelled and relevant, not decorative.
4.    Design implication / application - how the concept changes building design.
5.    Short conclusion - 1 or 2 lines linking back to comfort / climate responsiveness.

Source discipline
     Primary: Section A Lecture 1-11 slides and uploaded class notes.
     Question matching: Regular Final Term Question Bank 2016-2024 and the student question-analysis sheet.
     Reference check: Manual of Tropical Housing and Building; Climate & Design for the Built-form Designers.

     Correction policy যেখানে slide-এর wording বৈজ্ঞানিকভাবে oversimplified/ambiguous, সেখানে “Correction
     note” দিয়ে exam-safe wording ব্যবহার করা হয়েছে; মূল class framing বজায় রাখা হয়েছে।

LECTURE 01

Environment, Climate, Context & Comfort
মৌলিক ধারণা - যেখান থেকে প্রায় সব design question শুরু হয়

1. Environment and Man-made Environment
Environment is the overall physical condition in which we live and which can be perceived by the senses. A
human abode becomes a man-made environment because people intentionally modify natural conditions to
obtain shelter and comfort.
সহজ ভাষায়: প্রকৃ তি যেমন আছে সেটি “given”; মানুষ যখন ঘর, জানালা, ছাদ, ছায়া, ventilation ইত্যাদি দিয়ে নিজের

LECTURE 02

Climate & Built Environment: Ancient Wisdom,
Vitruvius and KHANA
Historical ideas interpreted as climate-responsive design principles

1. Why climate-responsive design is not a new movement
Ancient settlements already used orientation, slope, courtyards, wind protection, solar access and vegetation. The
central idea is timeless: a building should respond to the local environment instead of fighting it entirely with
mechanical systems.

Aristotle and Xenophon
   Aristotle: healthy cities benefit from east-inclined slopes and protection from harsh north winds.
   Xenophon: south-facing arrangements admit winter sun while high summer sun can be shaded by the
    roof/portico.

2. Human thermal comfort
The human body continuously produces heat through metabolism. Thermal comfort requires a steady thermal
state in which surplus heat is dissipated without excessive physiological strain.

                                  Core mechanisms: conduction, convection, radiation and evaporation.

Complexities
How a built-form designer translates climate data into design decisions

2. Essential knowledge
    Science of climate - temperature, radiation, wind, humidity and rainfall.
    Physiology - how the human body responds to heat/cold.
    Human comfort - acceptable ranges and subjective variables.
    Building materials - thermal capacity, insulation, moisture response, durability.
    Passive design technology - orientation, shading, ventilation, form, landscape.
    Active design technology - mechanical heating/cooling/ventilation when passive measures are insufficient.

Definitions, differences and short-note answers

1. Subject variables affecting comfort
Comfort is not determined by climate alone. Clothing, acclimatization, age and sex, body shape/fat, health,
food/drink and other personal factors modify thermal sensation.

4. Atmospheric depletion
Solar radiation is reduced while passing through the atmosphere by absorption and scattering due to ozone, water
vapour, dust, clouds and other particles. A longer atmospheric path generally means greater depletion.

pages.title: LECTURE 07 — Design Specifications: Layout, Spacing, Air
pages.text:
LECTURE 07

Design Specifications: Layout, Spacing, Air
Movement & Enclosure
The design-answer chapter: always draw

1. Design specification checklist
The lecture organizes climate-responsive design around five practical controls: Layout, Spacing, Air movement,
Enclosure and Shading Device.

    Shortcut L-S-A-E-S = Layout - Spacing - Air movement - Enclosure - Shading. মনে রাখো: “লেআউট-স্পেস-বাতাস-
    খোলস-ছায়া”.

2. Layout for wind and climate
    Broad spacing can improve breeze penetration in warm-humid climates.
    Staggered layout often avoids wind shadows and improves airflow through a group of buildings.
    Building orientation can be adjusted about 30-45 degrees to wind direction where suitable to improve
     exposure and flow distribution.
    In hot-dry/composite cases, compactness may reduce exposed surface area and unwanted heat gain; design
     must respond to season and climate type.

3. Spacing and functional distribution
    Organize functions according to heat, privacy, day/night use and air movement.
    Use floor height and internal voids/courtyards to support air movement and thermal stratification.
    Separate served and service zones where this helps buffer unwanted heat.

P/A ratio
For a given floor area, a compact form generally has a lower perimeter-to-area (P/A) ratio, which reduces exposed
envelope area. Circular/compact geometries have low P/A ratios, while highly articulated forms have higher
exposure.

4. Air movement and openings

5. Enclosure
   Material and thermal capacity determine heat storage and time lag.
   Degree of enclosure balances protection against the need for airflow.
   Insulation, roof build-up and external surface reflectance can reduce heat entry.

LECTURE 09

Shading Devices & Effective Shading
Solar control with orientation-sensitive sketches

1. Why shading?
The principal purpose of sun shading is to prevent unwanted solar radiation when external conditions are above
comfort level. Shading can also help control glare, rain exposure, privacy/visibility and sometimes wind direction.

                      Solar path into building                                                       Meaning

Direct radiation                                                      Beam radiation directly through an opening.

Reflected radiation                                                   Solar radiation reflected from ground/adjacent surfaces.

                                                                      Scattered sky radiation, important in cloudy/warm-humid
Diffuse radiation
                                                                      conditions.

                                                                      Solar heat absorbed by roof/wall and later conducted/radiated
Indirect through opaque surface
                                                                      inward.

2. External vs internal shading
External shading is generally more effective for heat control because it stops solar radiation before it passes
through the glazing and becomes indoor heat. Internal curtains can control glare but the absorbed solar heat is
already inside the envelope.

3. Rat-trap bond
Rat-trap bond places bricks on edge so that a cavity is created within the wall thickness. The lecture emphasizes
reduced material use, lower cost and improved thermal/sound insulation when correctly detailed.

                                                 Rat-trap bond conceptual plan / cavity sketch.

                         Construction rule                                                           Why it matters

Use consistent, good-quality bricks                                      Bond geometry depends on dimensional consistency.

Bottom and top courses solid                                             Stability and closure of cavity.

Sill/lintel and opening jamb zones solid                                 Allows frame fixing and local strength.

Reinforcement at corners/openings where designed                         Improves integrity / earthquake detailing.

Plan services through cavity carefully                                   Improves finish but must not weaken wall.

   Correction note The slide states wall strength is “not compromised”. Exam-safe wording: properly designed and
   constructed rat-trap masonry can provide adequate wall performance, but structural capacity depends on brick
   quality, workmanship, detailing and applicable code requirements.

LECTURE 11

Non-thermal Microclimate: Ventilation, Air Space,
Infiltration & Numericals
Formula-based preparation - do not leave this chapter for the exam hall

1. Objectives of ventilation / air change
   Supply adequate oxygen for breathing and other purposes.
   Remove carbon dioxide.
   Remove unwanted heat and moisture.
   Reduce staleness and smell / pollutants.

2. How ventilation rate is expressed

                                                     Core numerical relationship.

                                                    ACH = (Q x 3600) / V
                             Q in m3/s; V = room volume in m3. If Q is in L/s, first divide Q by 1000.

                       Air space per person = (net room volume) / number of users
            Net room volume may subtract major furniture/occupant volume if the problem specifically requires it.

3. Recommended air space and fresh-air supply (course table)
     Air space/person (m3)              Minimum (L/s/person)                 Smoking zone                 Non-smoking zone

3                                11.3                               22.6                           17.0

6                                7.1                                14.2                           10.7

                                                                                                                         Page
                                                                                                                       Page

9                                 5.2                               10.4                            7.8

12                                4.0                               8.0                             6.0

     Table-reading rule প্রথমে room volume / person থেকে air-space category নির্ধারণ করবে; তারপর smoking/non-
     smoking condition দেখে L/s/person নেবে; শেষে total Q = rate x number of persons.

4. Relative humidity numerical
                                                   RH = (AH / SH) x 100%
                                        Example: AH = 12 g/m3, SH = 17 g/m3 -> RH = 70.6%.

5. Ventilation numerical - worked example
Example: room 45 m x 23 m x 3 m, 200 persons, non-smoking. Volume V = 3105 m3, so air space/person = 15.525
m3. Using the highest listed 12 m3 category, the course table gives 6.0 L/s/person for a non-smoking zone.
11. Required fresh air = 200 x 6.0 = 1200 L/s = 1.20 m3/s.
12. ACH = 1.20 x 3600 / 3105 = 1.39 air changes/hour (approx.).

     Exam caution If the teacher expects interpolation or a different table-selection convention, follow the convention
     demonstrated in class. The uploaded table itself ends at 12 m3/person.

6. Heat loss due to air change
                             Heat loss rate = rho x Q x c_p x (T_inside - T_outside)
              Standard engineering form. If ACH is given: Q = ACH x V / 3600. rho is air density, c_p is specific heat.

     Standard engineering note যদি question-এ air density না দেওয়া থাকে, engineering calculations often use about
     1.2 kg/m3 near room conditions. এটি slide table-এর অংশ নয়; exam-এ teacher/class convention অনুসরণ করবে।

4. Common mistakes to avoid
    Do not write ET and CET as the same thing - CET includes radiation effect.
    Do not measure solar incidence angle from the surface itself in the cosine law; use the angle from the surface
     normal.
    Do not claim air movement always cools by lowering air temperature - it improves convection/evaporation
     and changes perceived comfort.
    Do not use KHANA rules as universal modern codes - state the Bengal/Bangladesh climatic context.
    Do not draw shading devices without showing sun direction / blocked ray.
    In ventilation numericals, convert L/s to m3/s before using ACH formula.
    Always state units.
